item.title: Psychological mechanisms of perceived technological dependence on generative artificial intelligence tools: perceived knowledge, trust, anxiety, and self-efficacy
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative AI tools are increasingly used in design education, yet the relationship between students’ perceptions of these tools and their reported reliance on them remains unclear. This study analyzed cross-sectional survey responses from 526 undergraduate students in design-related disciplines using partial least squares structural equation modeling. In the specified model, perceived reliability, perceived usefulness, and perceived intelligence were positively associated with perceived AIGC knowledge, whereas perceived ease of use was not significantly associated with it. Perceived AIGC knowledge was positively associated with trust, self-efficacy, and usage intention and negatively associated with AIGC-related anxiety. Trust, AIGC-related anxiety, and self-efficacy each showed a significant indirect effect in the modeled relationship between perceived AIGC knowledge and usage intention. Usage intention was strongly associated with perceived technological dependence. These findings are consistent with the proposed framework, but the cross-sectional data do not establish the temporal sequence of the constructs or show that reported dependence reflects harmful overuse. The study extends technology acceptance research by examining perceived reliance in AIGC-supported creative work.

item.title: Gendered affective representations in AI-assisted music videos: a qualitative multimethod study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly visible in music-video production, influencing both production practices and the ways in which emotion, bodies, and gender are portrayed visually. This study examines gendered emotional representation in AI-assisted music videos. Methods A qualitative multimethod design combined interpretive visual analysis of four purposively selected AI-assisted music videos with asynchronous written expert interviews involving six creative-industry professionals and four psychology experts ( N = 10). The videos were analysed through an interpretive coding framework covering emotion, gender, body and face, power relations, AI aesthetics, and traces of bias. Results Across the cases, emotion was conveyed not only through facial expression but also through atmosphere, colour, movement, editing, and spatial transitions. The selected works sometimes reproduced familiar conventions, including heteronormative intimacy, militarised masculinity, and idealised female bodies, but also unsettled them through female anger and solidarity and mutable synthetic bodies. Ambiguity in a body’s appearance did not necessarily unsettle its gendered narrative role. Industry accounts described how prompting, selection, revision, and post-production shape representations, while general psychology-expert perspectives informed their interpretation. Discussion The findings position AI-assisted music videos as co-produced sites of synthetic visual culture in which established gendered conventions may be repeated, negotiated, or challenged. Neither expert group provided direct evidence about the production or reception of the selected videos. The findings underline the practical importance of representational review, consent, diversity, and transparent disclosure in AI-assisted cultural production.

item.title: Parasocial and interpersonal interaction: distinct associations with customer value co-creation in virtual brand communities
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Virtual brand communities expose members to communication from the brand side and interaction with other members, but these sources may not relate to participation through the same psychological processes. Drawing on the stimulus organism response framework, social identity theory, and social cognitive theory, this study tested whether community identification and self-efficacy statistically accounted for indirect associations between parasocial interaction, interpersonal interaction, and customer value co-creation behavior. The hypotheses were examined in an unpublished cross-sectional survey of 240 adult users of virtual brand communities in China. An audit of the questionnaire and data codebook corrected a prior item-block parsing error and established the intended 30-item measurement structure. Internal consistency was acceptable for the five composites (Cronbach's alpha = 0.730–0.837; McDonald's omega = 0.744–0.838). A five-factor confirmatory model fit better than models combining the interaction constructs, combining the mediators, or placing all items on one factor, although its absolute fit and discriminant validity were only partly satisfactory (CFI = 0.870, TLI = 0.857, RMSEA = 0.064, SRMR = 0.056). Regression estimates used HC3 robust standard errors, and indirect associations used 5,000 percentile-bootstrap samples. Parasocial interaction uniquely predicted community identification and self-efficacy, and both variables were associated with customer value co-creation. The indirect associations of parasocial interaction through community identification ( B = 0.163, 95% CI [0.038, 0.303]) and self-efficacy ( B = 0.167, 95% CI [0.053, 0.281]) were statistically detectable. Interpersonal interaction retained a direct association with customer value co-creation but did not uniquely predict either proposed mediator when both interaction variables were included; its two specific indirect associations were not statistically detectable. Results were similar after excluding uniform responders and after adding demographic and community-use controls. The findings distinguish relational and capability-related correlates of parasocial interaction while showing that interpersonal interaction may share substantial variance with brand-side relational experience. Because the data are cross-sectional, same-source, and affected by incomplete discriminant validity, the indirect effects are interpreted as covariance patterns consistent with the proposed pathways rather than evidence of causal psychological mechanisms.

item.title: Prompt specificity and iterative behaviour in text-to-music co-creation: a secondary analysis of interaction logs and a framework for perceived creative control
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence can lower barriers to musical creation while also shifting consequential decisions away from the user. Methods This study examines that tension through a secondary analysis of the published PAGURI interaction-log prompt corpus and develops a tentative framework for perceived creative control. The analysable corpus contained 304 text-to-music prompts from 24 participants. Musical specificity was operationalised as explicit instrument and technical-parameter markers; iterative continuity was measured with Jaccard similarity between consecutive prompts and checked against TF-IDF cosine similarity. To avoid pseudoreplication, group comparisons were conducted on participant-level summaries rather than treating 304 prompts as independent cases. Results Role-derived experience groups differed substantially in mean prompt specificity, H(2) = 10.25, p = 0.006, ε 2 = 0.39, and specificity density, H(2) = 11.52, p = 0.003, ε 2 = 0.45, but not in refinement rate, H(2) = 0.24, p = 0.888. At a descriptive Jaccard threshold of 0.20, 46.8% of consecutive pairs were refinements and 53.2% were restarts; because this classification was threshold-sensitive, continuous similarity remained the primary continuity measure. Prompt specificity did not increase systematically across the session: the mean within-person Spearman correlation was ρ = −0.06, and the distribution of participant-level correlations did not differ significantly from zero, W = 89.0, p = 0.374. Discussion These findings distinguish the explicit technical-musical information users encode in prompts from the sequential continuity of their prompting behaviour. The paper integrates task structure, system autonomy, model coverage, prior experience, self-efficacy, and psychological ownership into a testable framework for future music-education research. Given the small participant-level sample and role-derived grouping, the empirical findings are exploratory and require confirmation in larger, controlled studies.

item.title: How AI disclosure influences consumers' purchase intention toward AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion: the roles of perceived usefulness, perceived authenticity, and algorithm aversion
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background With the growing application of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in fashion design and cultural and creative industries, AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion has created new opportunities for the contemporary transformation of traditional culture. However, whether consumers are willing to accept such products and how AI disclosure influences their evaluations and purchase intentions remain unclear. Drawing on the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) model, this study examines the mechanisms through which AI disclosure, design aesthetics, cultural identity, perceived usefulness, perceived authenticity, and algorithm aversion influence consumers' purchase intentions toward AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion. Methods A questionnaire survey combined with a scenario-based experiment was employed. Six AI-generated fashion illustrations derived from Tujia costume elements were developed and selected as stimulus materials. Participants were randomly assigned to either an AI disclosure group or a non-disclosure group. Data were collected through Tencent Questionnaire, yielding 410 valid responses. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Importance–Performance Map Analysis (IPMA) were employed to examine the structural relationships, mediating effects, moderating effects, and practical priorities for improvement. Results Design aesthetics and cultural identity influenced purchase intention through perceived usefulness and perceived authenticity, with perceived usefulness emerging as the strongest predictor of purchase intention. AI disclosure significantly reduced design aesthetics, cultural identity, perceived usefulness, and perceived authenticity. Algorithm aversion did not significantly moderate the relationship between perceived usefulness and purchase intention but significantly strengthened the positive effect of perceived authenticity on purchase intention. Conclusions This study reveals the multiple psychological pathways through which AI disclosure shapes consumers' evaluations of AI-generated ethnic cultural fashion. The findings further indicate that algorithm aversion alters the extent to which consumers rely on authenticity judgments when forming purchase intentions. This study extends the application of the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) model to the context of AI-generated cultural products and provides practical implications for balancing AI transparency, cultural authenticity, and the practical value of products.

item.title: Generative AI as a team moderator in CSCL : Facilitating students' multidimensional engagement through adaptive scaffolding for socially shared regulation of learning
item.description:
British Journal of Educational Technology
Abstract Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is essential for successful collaboration, yet effectively scaffolding it remains challenging because regulatory needs are dynamic and context‐dependent. While generative AI (GenAI) offers potential for adaptive support, current applications in collaborative learning largely position it as a content‐oriented tutor for knowledge explanation or idea generation, leaving its role as a process‐oriented team moderator for scaffolding SSRL processes underexplored. To address this gap, we conducted a 16‐week quasi‐experiment with 64 undergraduates in China, comparing adaptive SSRL scaffolding delivered by a GenAI agent in the adaptive‐SSRL condition with static scaffolding via structured digital worksheets in the static‐SSRL condition. Survey data and group discussion transcripts were analysed using statistical methods and epistemic network analysis. Results indicated several differences in students' multidimensional engagement between the two conditions: (1) Behaviourally, the adaptive‐SSRL group showed significantly higher participation equality, although participation intensity did not differ significantly between groups. (2) Cognitively, the adaptive‐SSRL group demonstrated deeper cognitive engagement, reflected in more advanced cognitive presence phases and more integrative, solution‐oriented discourse patterns. (3) Emotionally, the adaptive‐SSRL group reported significantly higher overall emotional engagement, particularly feeling more relaxed during collaboration and more connected with peers. These findings extend human–AI collaboration research by showing that GenAI can function as an SSRL‐informed team moderator rather than a content‐oriented tutor. They also offer design implications for GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding and human–AI role division in CSCL. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is critical for successful collaboration and is closely associated with the quality of student engagement. While static scaffolds (eg, worksheets) provide a basic regulatory structure, they fail to adapt to the dynamic and emergent needs of collaborating teams. Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used for personalised content support, yet its potential as a process‐oriented team moderator remains underexplored. What this paper adds This study introduced SSRLAgent, a GenAI agent grounded in SSRL theory and established principles of collective metacognitive support, to provide adaptive and interactive regulatory scaffolding. In a 16‐week quasi‐experiment, we compared GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding (SSRLAgent) with static scaffolding (structured digital worksheets) in CSCL. Adaptive‐SSRL scaffolding was associated with higher‐quality engagement: greater participation equality, deeper cognitive engagement and higher overall emotional engagement. Implications for practice and/or policy The study underscores the necessity of shifting SSRL scaffolding from static, ‘one‐size‐fits‐all’ support to adaptive GenAI interventions to improve collaborative engagement. The findings provide design guidance for developing SSRL agents that are embedded in the shared interaction space and responsive to groups' moment‐to‐moment regulatory needs. The study suggests a productive human–AI division of labour: GenAI agents can support process coordination and regulatory prompting, while teachers and peers remain essential for relationally complex forms of support that collaborative learning requires.

item.title: The mediating role of artificial intelligence perception and creative idea generation in the impact of sustainable leadership on digital transformation and circular economy awareness
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Today, sustainable leadership is a strategic leadership approach that addresses environmental, social, and economic priorities from a holistic perspective while at the same time driving digital transformation processes. The research aims to explain how sustainable leaders mobilize organizational resources, technological infrastructure, and human creativity within the framework of Dynamic Capabilities Theory. Methods The research was conducted on 456 white-collar employees working in small and medium-sized enterprises operating in Giresun, Kars, and Kırşehir provinces. The data collected by the convenience sampling method were analyzed using the PLS-SEM method with the SmartPLS 4.1.1 program. Results The analysis results show that sustainable leadership has significant and positive effects on perceptions of artificial intelligence, the generation of creative ideas, digital transformation, and awareness of the circular economy. It was found that the perception of artificial intelligence (AI) has a significant effect on both digital transformation and awareness of the circular economy. It was also determined that creative idea generation has significant effects on digital transformation and awareness of the circular economy. The results of the mediation analyses revealed a partial mediating role for all variables. Discussion The findings reveal that sustainable leadership is not limited to the environmental and social responsibility dimension and is a strategic element that directs digital transformation processes, shapes perceptions towards artificial intelligence, and encourages organizational creativity.

item.title: Thinking, Feeling, and Acting with Generative AI: Affective, Behavioral, and Cognitive Engagement and Perceived Human–AI Outcomes
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
Generative AI requires students not only to adopt technology but also to engage critically, behaviorally, cognitively, and emotionally with its outputs. This study develops and tests the AI Engagement ABC+ Model, a domain-specific adaptation of the affective–behavioral–cognitive engagement framework. The model differentiates positive and negative AI affect, three behavioral functions, creation, verification, and community participation, and two cognitive regulatory functions, strategic and critical cognition. A cross-sectional online survey collected data from 1250 students representing 15 nationalities at eight universities in China. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was used to examine 15 hypothesized associations between seven first-order engagement facets and four self-reported AI-supported outcomes: perceived Output Quality, Creativity, Integrity, and Trust Calibration. Fourteen hypotheses were supported. Verification Behavior had the largest estimated coefficient among the included predictors of Integrity (β = 0.303) and perceived Output Quality (β = 0.269) and was also associated with perceived Trust Calibration (β = 0.191). Critical Cognition had the largest estimated coefficient among the included predictors of perceived Trust Calibration (β = 0.270), and Community Behavior was positively associated with Integrity (β = 0.290) and Creativity (β = 0.240). Positive AI Affect was associated with perceived Output Quality (β = 0.214) and Creativity (β = 0.139), whereas Negative AI Affect was negatively associated with Trust Calibration (β = −0.137) but was unrelated to Integrity. The model explained 25.7% of the variance in Creativity, 25.2% in Integrity, 20.8% in perceived Output Quality, and 17.6% in Trust Calibration. Positive Q2_predict values provided additional evidence of out-of-sample predictive relevance. The findings support a differentiated view of GenAI engagement in which specific affective, behavioral, and cognitive facets are associated with distinct perceived outcomes. The model offers a theoretically structured basis for further research on responsible GenAI engagement, while its cross-sectional self-report design precludes causal or objective-performance conclusions.

item.title: The Impact of the Integration of Artificial Intelligence and Search Technology on Online Purchase Intentions
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
Based on Service-Dominant Logic (SDL) theory, this study surveyed 409 users who had used Taobao’s AI Universal Search and used structural equation modeling to explore the mechanisms through which AI-integrated search technology promotes online purchase intention. The findings indicate that AI and search technology influence customers’ purchase intent through value co-creation, personalization, and decision-making time. Based on the structural equation model, the study compares the extent to which decision-making time and value co-creation factors influence purchase intention. The research offers practical implications for the platform economy by highlighting the enabling effects of large language models and the provision of precise supply-demand matching. The results indicate that platforms should optimize AI search results to reduce customers’ decision-making time.

item.title: Unlocking Breakthrough Innovation: The Impact of Knowledge Co-creation and Contractual Knowledge Protection
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
There are relatively few existing studies that provide references for Chinese local firms to use collaboration to carry out breakthrough innovation. This study was conducted on 306 respondents from 153 Chinese manufacturing firms, and results indicate that knowledge co-creation mediates the link between resource complementarity and breakthrough innovation. Crucially, the analysis reveals a mediated moderation mechanism: the synergistic interaction between complementarity and contractual knowledge protection is transmitted via knowledge co-creation to drive innovation outcomes. These findings provide insights for firms that want to carry out collaborative breakthrough innovation but are not sure about partner selection and implementation mechanisms in Chinese settings.

item.title: Research on Human-AI Collaboration Based on BERTopic: Exploratory Thematic Mapping and Evolutionary Analysis (2020-2025)
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
With the increasing integration of artificial intelligence across various societal domains, research on human-AI collaboration has grown rapidly in recent years. This study adopts a thematic mapping approach based on the BERTopic modeling framework to examine the structural organization and evolutionary dynamics of the core human-AI collaboration literature from 2020 to 2025. The analysis identifies nine core themes, including creative collaboration, which are further grouped into four higher-level thematic clusters, such as "Cognitive and Knowledge Co-creation". Longitudinal results show that, although publication output has increased substantially over time, the overall distribution of thematic structures remains relatively stable. This stability suggests a pattern of proportional development across themes, providing a macro-level perspective for understanding the conceptual organization and evolution of the field.

item.title: Mapping generative AI in higher education teaching and learning: a scoping review
item.description:
International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly entered higher education, but empirical research on its roles in teaching and learning remains fragmented across instructional activities, outcomes, assessment approaches, and stakeholder perspectives. This scoping review followed PRISMA-ScR guidelines to map 394 empirical studies of GenAI use in higher education published from November 2022 through December 2025. The review examined how GenAI tools were integrated into authentic teaching and learning activities, what outcomes or skills were targeted, how studies assessed those outcomes, and how students and instructors perceived GenAI use. Across the reviewed studies, GenAI was most often used to support existing academic tasks, especially feedback, tutoring, and writing. The most frequently targeted outcomes included engagement, usability and acceptance, critical thinking, disciplinary knowledge, academic performance, writing quality, and AI literacy. Self-regulated learning, ethics, creativity, feedback quality, and equity received less attention. Assessment practices relied mainly on surveys, tests or rubrics, artifact analysis, and interviews, suggesting that much of the evidence base is shaped by short-term and readily implemented methods. Student and instructor perceptions were predominantly mixed, reflecting perceived benefits alongside concerns about pedagogy, integrity, workload, and governance. The review highlights the need for stronger alignment between learning constructs and assessment methods, more process-sensitive evidence, clearer reporting of governance practices, and greater attention to equity in GenAI-supported higher education. Supplementary Information: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00630-9.

item.title: Generative artificial intelligence literacy profiles differ in academic self-efficacy and subjective well-being among adolescents
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is increasingly important for adolescents, yet variation in literacy across multiple dimensions and its associations with educational and psychological outcomes remain insufficiently understood. This study identified generative AI literacy profiles among Korean adolescents with generative AI experience ( N = 3,959) using K-means cluster analysis based on information evaluation, communication, creative use, and ethical use. Two profiles were identified: Higher AI Literacy and Lower AI Literacy. The profiles differed primarily in their overall literacy levels rather than in qualitatively distinct patterns across the four dimensions. Adolescents in the Higher AI Literacy profile reported greater generative AI education experience and higher academic self-efficacy and subjective well-being than those in the Lower AI Literacy profile. Differences in academic self-efficacy and subjective well-being remained significant after adjustment for gender, school level, academic achievement, and economic status. These findings demonstrate meaningful level-based variation in generative AI literacy among adolescents with generative AI experience and suggest that such variation is associated with educational experience and academic and psychological outcomes. A person-centred perspective may complement variable-centred approaches and inform future research and educational approaches that consider differences in students’ generative AI literacy levels.

item.title: Comprehensive artificial intelligence-assisted mental health program for university students in China (CAMPUS): study protocol for a multi-center prospective cohort with planned embedded randomized intervention trials
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
University students face a rising prevalence of depression, anxiety, insomnia, and suicidal ideation that exceeds the capacity of conventional, resource-constrained campus support services. Although artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted screening tools have emerged, many have evaluated selected modalities or isolated prediction tasks, and their integration with prospectively evaluated intervention pathways remains limited. This protocol describes the Comprehensive Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Mental Health Program for University Students in China (CAMPUS), a multi-center research program comprising a five-year prospective cohort, eight planned embedded randomized controlled trials, and exploratory multimodal AI and multi-omics studies across seven Chinese universities. Longitudinal cohort enrolment commenced at Henan Medical University in September 2025 and is planned to expand across seven participating universities. Multidimensional screening integrates psychological self-report (PHQ-9, GAD-7, ISI, BSI-CV, and others), physiological measurements (EEG, MRI, fNIRS, HRV, eye tracking, facial-expression analysis, ERP, voice acoustics), and an exploratory biospecimen component for multi-omics profiling, potentially including genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and microbiome analyses, subject to the finalization and approval of layer-specific protocols. Students identified through cohort screening as potentially eligible for an intervention trial will undergo trial-specific eligibility assessment. Those who meet the eligibility criteria and provide trial-specific informed consent will be individually randomized in a 1:1 ratio to the intervention or its comparator within one of eight separate two-arm, multi-center, parallel-group randomized controlled trials. A Transformer-based multimodal AI framework with SHAP-based feature attribution will be developed and internally evaluated for questionnaire-defined risk stratification and exploratory treatment-response prediction. The initial Henan Medical University cohort recruitment and university-student mental-health assessment were approved by the Ethics Review Committee of Henan Medical University (XYLL-20250484), and written informed consent is obtained from participants before enrolment. Each additional participating center will obtain local ethics approval before study activation. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, scientific conferences, and policy briefs, providing evidence that may inform the design and prospective evaluation of youth mental-health programs in other university settings. Clinical trial registration The two clinical trials were registered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR). The registration details and URLs are as follows: ChiCTR2500113527: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=298271 ; ChiCTR2500113613: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=298268 .

item.title: Exploration or exploitation? The double-edged effects of AI use modes on radical creativity: evidence from AI-enabled drug discovery
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely adopted in corporate innovation activities, yet prior research has not reached a consensus on whether it is more conducive to incremental or radical innovation. For radical innovation, which depends on highly novel ideas, realizing the value of AI depends not only on whether AI is adopted but, more importantly, on whether employees can use it creatively to transcend established knowledge boundaries. Drawing on environmental dynamism and the exploration–exploitation perspective, this study develops a theoretical model linking leaders’ perceptions of environmental dynamism, employees’ AI use modes, leader temporal myopia, and employee radical creativity in the context of AI-enabled drug discovery. We distinguish leaders’ perceptions of environmental dynamism into perceived technological dynamism and perceived market dynamism, and employees’ AI use into exploratory and exploitative AI use. The model is tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling and three-wave matched survey data from 368 leader–employee dyads. The results show that leader-perceived technological dynamism is positively associated with employee exploratory AI use, whereas leader-perceived market dynamism is positively associated with employee exploitative AI use. Exploratory AI use is positively associated with employee radical creativity, whereas exploitative AI use is negatively associated with it. Leader temporal myopia weakens the positive conditional indirect relationship of technological dynamism with radical creativity through exploratory AI use and strengthens the negative conditional indirect relationship of market dynamism with radical creativity through exploitative AI use. By adopting a knowledge-activity perspective, this study reveals the differentiated relationships between AI use modes and radical creativity and further explains how perceptions of the external environment, leaders’ temporal orientation, and employees’ AI use behaviors are differentially related. The findings provide a theoretical basis and practical implications for helping firms engaged in AI-enabled drug discovery guide employees toward effective AI use and enhance radical creativity.

item.title: Developing computational thinking in teacher education: a brief experience with coding, robotics, and machine learning
item.description:
Educational Technology Research and Development
Abstract This study examines post-intervention self-reported outcomes associated with a short intervention designed to introduce coding, educational robotics, and introductory concepts of machine learning into initial teacher education for Primary Education. The proposal is grounded in Papert’s principles and the Creative and Computational Problem Solving model, combining active learning methodologies with accessible technologies. A quasi-experimental design with a non-equivalent control group was employed. A total of 144 first-year students from three Spanish universities participated (105 in the experimental group and 39 in the control group). The intervention consisted of a two-hour workshop with hands-on stations and technological challenges, designed as a feasible microintervention within regular teacher education contexts. Assessment was carried out through an ad hoc questionnaire focused on three dimensions: knowledge of programming and machine learning, block-based programming and game engines, and active learning, all assessed through self-reported perceptions. The results showed statistically significant post-intervention differences in favor of the experimental group, with a small effect size for knowledge of programming and machine learning and large effect sizes for block-based programming and game engines and active learning. Item-level analyses revealed that favorable overall perceptions coexisted with lower self-reported familiarity in specific technical areas, particularly machine learning, prior experience with block-based programming, and programming in game engines. Three exploratory response profiles were also identified: reluctant, intermediate, and enthusiastic. The findings suggest that well-structured microinterventions may support higher self-reported knowledge of programming and machine learning, greater familiarity with block-based programming and game engines, and more positive perceptions of active learning in teacher education.

item.title: Behavioral differentiation during the AIGC image generation waiting period: effects on creativity in conceptual design
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction: Artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) offers new ways to generate inspiration for conceptual design, yet limited attention has been paid to the waiting period between prompt submission and AI image output. This study examined behavioral differentiation during this interval and investigated how the task relevance and cognitive load of waiting-period behaviors affect creativity in conceptual design. Methods Three experiments were conducted with design students. Experiment 1 identified and classified core waiting-period behaviors ( N = 30); Experiment 2 measured the cognitive load of representative behaviors using the NASA-TLX ( N = 24); and Experiment 3 employed a behavior-based 2 × 2 conceptual framework ( N = 60), in which four representative waiting-period behaviors were selected to represent different combinations of task relevance (high/low) and relative workload (higher/lower), and their creative performance was compared. Results The results showed that the AIGC generation waiting period was not a passive interval but involved multiple identifiable behavioral patterns. Creative performance differed across the four representative behavioral conditions. Specifically, the overall creativity score in the GP condition was significantly lower than the scores in the RS, DB, and RB conditions, whereas no significant differences were observed among the latter three conditions. These findings further suggest that the subsequent influence of waiting-period behaviors on creativity may depend not only on the level of cognitive demand but also on whether cognitive resources remain directed toward the ongoing creative task. Discussion This study further interprets AIGC generation waiting-period behaviors from three interrelated functional perspectives: task continuity, cognitive expenditure, and temporary disengagement/incubation. This functional account provides an empirical basis for understanding the cognitive role of the AIGC generation waiting period and for optimizing AI-assisted conceptual design workflows.

item.title: The impact of human-AI co-creation on perceived creativity in generative AI art: a serial mediation mechanism of psychological ownership, perceived agency, and creative flow
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative AI is shifting digital art from one-step generation toward interactive human-AI co-creation. Across two between-subject experiments ( N = 600), we examined how creation mode and prespecified AI-involvement workflows related to perceived creativity. Methods In Study 1, participants completed digital art tasks under human-only creation, AI-only generation, or human-AI co-creation conditions. In Study 2, three workflows differing in AI involvement (low, moderate, high) were evaluated. Psychological ownership, perceived agency, creative flow, and perceived creativity were measured. Results In Study 1, human-AI co-creation produced higher perceived-creativity ratings than AI-only generation, with indirect effects consistent with a serial pathway through psychological ownership, perceived agency, and creative flow. In Study 2, the moderate-involvement workflow yielded higher perceived-creativity ratings and psychological states than the low- and high-involvement workflows. Discussion Perceived creativity in generative-AI art depends on how users experience contribution, control, and engagement during creation. Within the workflows tested, balancing generative assistance with consequential user choice fosters the most favorable subjective creativity evaluations.

item.title: The invisible signature: Top-down bias in aesthetic evaluation of visual and textual AI-generated art
item.description:
Computers in Human Behavior Reports
The rapid evolution of generative AI has blurred the boundaries between human and machine art making, raising questions about how authorship information shapes the evaluation of creative products. This study extends previous research by examining how attributed authorship influences the evaluation of genuinely AI-generated art by directly comparing expressive modalities, namely prose (ChatGPT) and images (DALL·E), while also accounting for participant- and stimulus-related characteristics. Participants (N = 121 Italian adults) first evaluated stimuli under a blind baseline condition and then a different, balanced set accompanied by an explicit human- or AI-attribution label. Mixed repeated-measures GLMs examined whether evaluations changed from baseline to disclosure as a function of attributed authorship; educational level and perceived complexity were then entered stepwise as covariates to assess whether the observed pattern was sensitive to participant- and stimulus-related variability, respectively. Across models, evaluations decreased following AI attribution, whereas they remained stable following human attribution. Before covariate adjustment, the baseline-to-disclosure decrease was stronger for texts than for images and varied across evaluative dimensions, with the largest decreases observed for subjective and objective aesthetic judgments, a smaller near-threshold change for emotion, and comparatively stable originality. After educational level and perceived complexity were taken into account, modality- and dimension-related differences were no longer evident in the final model, suggesting that these effects were partly intertwined with characteristics of the participants and stimuli. By contrast, the differential response to attributed authorship persisted after adjustment. These findings confirm that source attribution exerts a robust top-down influence on the appraisal of AI-generated creative products, while differences across expressive modalities and evaluative dimensions provide a more fine-grained account of how this influence is expressed within aesthetic evaluation.

item.title: GenAI-supported project-based product design learning: differential changes in multidimensional learning outcomes
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in design education, yet evidence remains limited on whether its educational value derives from tool access itself or from how human–AI interaction is structured within project work. This quasi-experimental pre-test–post-test study compared a 4-week GenAI-Integrated Project-Based Learning Module (GIPLM) with traditional project-based learning (PjBL) in an undergraduate product design course ( N = 60). Rather than treating GenAI as a stand-alone content-generation tool, GIPLM embedded GenAI as process scaffolding across four stages: product and requirement analysis, user research and knowledge structuring, ideation with multimodal visualization and 3D prototyping, and feedback, validation, and reflective presentation. Learning outcomes were assessed across cognitive, affective, and psychomotor-related domains, together with course performance. According to a mixed-design ANOVA, the GenAI-supported group was associated with significantly greater gains than the control group in cognitive understanding, problem-solving and creativity, fundamental tool operation, advanced design application, and final academic performance. Because advanced design application differed at baseline, ANCOVA was additionally conducted; the post-test group effect remained significant after controlling for pre-test scores, F (1, 57) = 20.519, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.265. Engagement and participation and ethical and user-centered responsibility improved over time but showed no significant Time × Group interactions. These findings suggest that the observed advantages are more consistent with structured, workflow-embedded GenAI scaffolding than with AI access alone, with stronger short-term effects on cognitive, procedural, and performance outcomes than on affective development.

item.title: Psychological associations between perceived generative AI-supported learning and creative design performance in vocational design education: a within-course correlational study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in design courses, but evidence remains limited on how students’ appraisal of such support co-varies with domain cognition, creative confidence, engagement, and independently assessed creative work. This within-course correlational study examined within-course change and theory-specified contemporaneous associations in a 72-h Furniture Appreciation and Selection course involving 150 vocational design students in China. Sustainable design cognition and creative self-efficacy were measured before and after the course; perceived GenAI-supported learning and learning engagement were measured after it; and final creative design performance was rated independently by three experts. Paired-samples t tests described within-course change. Item-level CFA preceded the score-level association analyses, while standardized composite-score ordinary least squares models and 10,000-resample percentile bootstrap confidence intervals summarized theory-specified post-course associations and coefficient products. Sustainable design cognition increased from 3.326 to 3.792, t (149) = 10.362, p < 0.001, d z = 0.846, and creative self-efficacy increased from 3.509 to 3.877, t (149) = 7.424, p < 0.001, d z = 0.606; these values indicate change during the course as a whole rather than a GenAI-specific intervention effect. Among the direct post-course associations, learning engagement showed the largest coefficient with expert-rated creative design performance (β = 0.515, p < 0.001; f 2 = 0.361). The theory-specified coefficient products were 0.076 for SDC-CSE-LE, 0.204 for CSE-LE-CP, and 0.0080 for AISL-SDC-CSE-LE-CP. The last interval narrowly excluded zero [0.0002, 0.0234], but the product was statistically detectable and negligible in magnitude. Because the study followed one cohort without a comparison condition and most model variables were measured at the same post-course occasion, the findings support within-course change and contemporaneous association, not causal or temporally ordered effects.

item.title: Social cognitive communication mechanism of digital participation in Chinese traditional music in the context of cultural identity and intangible cultural heritage
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Digital platforms have reshaped how traditional Chinese music circulates, yet the psychological mechanism linking user participation to cultural identification remains undertheorized. Drawing together social cognitive theory, contemporary cultural psychology, and communication theory, this study develops a four-layer architecture (input, participation, cognitive, and identity) coupled with a staged process model spanning information encoding, symbolic decoding, cognitive reconstruction, and identity internalization. A hybrid specification formalizes the mechanism, pairing structural equation modeling with attention-weighted neural aggregation; both components are estimated and validated on the same data. Empirical testing draws on 2,346 behavioral records from music, short-form video, and social media platforms, paired with 1,128 survey responses from users engaged with the guqin, Kunqu, pipa, and regional opera repertoires. Item loadings, heterotrait-monotrait ratios, collinearity diagnostics, and a common-method check document measurement quality. Results indicate that digital participation (DP) shapes cultural identity (CI) mainly through social cognitive communication (SCC), with the co-creation and dissemination strata showing indirect effects that are more than three times those of passive exposure. As the direct participation-identity path remains significant, the pattern is one of partial rather than full mediation. Cultural identity also looks more like a hinge than a terminal state: a chained specification linking identification to downstream cognitive engagement returns a reliable indirect path, which is consistent with the recursive reading the framework proposes but, on single-wave evidence, cannot establish it. Community climate exerts the strongest moderating influence, exceeding both platform affordance and content polish. Since the design is cross-sectional, all of these patterns are read as associations rather than as causal effects; even so, they suggest that audience cultivation and co-creation tooling deserve at least as much investment as interface refinement in the digitization of traditional music.

item.title: How Agent-Driven Creative Trace Mining Reshapes Design Behavior in a Deployment Study of Intent-Aligned Multimodal Design
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Designers continuously capture inspirations across media, yet these creative traces remain underutilized in computational design support. We present DesignJournal, an agent-driven system that mines multimodal creative traces and transforms them into intent-aligned image generation. The system consolidates artifacts into a unified workspace and employs an agentic pipeline for structured grouping, belief-guided prompt refinement, and iterative intent updates. We developed a framework that classifies sequential design actions, deriving a hierarchical action taxonomy from interaction logs. We used it to examine how agent affordances reshape design behavior. A 10-day deployment study with eight professional designers compared baseline and agent-supported conditions across 5838 classified actions. Agent support significantly reduced the frequency of spatial repositioning actions, particularly small-distance movements, while sequential transition structures shifted from extended repositioning chains toward relational encoding sequences. Awareness of agent interpretation shaped upstream recording behavior, and agent-mediated collaboration extended designers’ creative reach beyond independent exploration.

item.title: Pedagogical GenAI use and self-reported creative cognition in art education: a three-wave time-lagged correlational study among design students
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in design education, yet the psychological pathways associated with students' self-reported creative cognition remain unclear. In this three-wave time-lagged correlational study, 389 design students at a South Korean university reported pedagogical GenAI use at Wave 1, creative self-efficacy and AI-related learning anxiety at Wave 2, and creative engagement and self-reported creative cognition at Wave 3. Pedagogical GenAI use referred to coursework-related use for ideation, style exploration, revision, comparison of alternatives, and feedback seeking. Covariance-based structural equation modeling showed good fit [comparative fit index (CFI) = 0.983, root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) = 0.026]. Higher GenAI use was associated with higher self-efficacy (β = 0.489) and lower anxiety (β = -0.191). The total modeled association with self-reported creative cognition was β = 0.456 [95% CI [0.314, 0.604]]; its indirect components constituted approximately 59%. The GenAI-origin serial indirect association through self-efficacy and engagement was β = 0.122, whereas the corresponding anxiety-engagement association was β = 0.015. Separately, self-efficacy was indirectly associated with creative cognition through engagement (β = 0.249); this quantity does not include the preceding GenAI-use path. Because the study was observational and engagement and cognition were measured concurrently at Wave 3, the findings do not identify causal mediation. They are consistent with an appraisal-to-engagement account in which competence beliefs have a larger modeled role than anxiety reduction.

item.title: The domain-specific bias in creativity evaluation: human evaluators favor human-created art, but prefer AI outputs for divergent thinking
item.description:
BMC Psychology
Abstract How do humans perceive and evaluate creativity when it is attributed to artificial intelligence (AI)? This research examined how labeling a source as “AI” versus “human” systematically biases creativity evaluations across different domains. In experiment 1 (painting and poetry), outputs labeled as human-created were rated as more creative than identical AI-labeled outputs in artistic creation. Experiment 2, which manipulated the attribution of co-created works, revealed that the “human ideation with AI assistance” label enhanced perceived originality in poetry, whereas those attributed primarily to humans remained dominant in evaluations of painting. Experiment 3 utilized a divergent thinking task (Alternative Uses Test), found a reversal: the same output received higher creativity ratings when bearing an AI label. The findings reveal a domain-specific pattern in attitudes toward AI creativity: viewing collaboration positively yet maintaining a persistent bias in valuing AI’s creative contributions.

item.title: The relationship between challenge-hindrance stressors and AI dependence among art students: the mediating roles of creative self-efficacy and positive experiences
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Despite growing concerns about art students’ over-reliance on generative AI tools, existing research has largely treated academic stress as a uniform construct, overlooking the possibility that different types of stressors may drive AI dependence through distinct psychological pathways. Methods Based on the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution (I-PACE) model, this study examines the relationships between Challenge-Hindrance stressors (CHS) and AI dependence among art students. It explores the mediating roles of creative self-efficacy and positive experiences. A questionnaire survey was conducted among 580 art students using the Challenge-Hindrance Stress Scale, the Creative Self-Efficacy Scale, the Positive Experiences Scale, and the AI Dependence Scale. Results Path analysis revealed that both challenge stressors ( β = 0.245, p < 0.001) and hindrance stressors ( β = 0.322, p < 0.001) were positively associated with AI dependence; challenge stressors were negatively associated with creative self-efficacy ( β = −0.155, p = 0.003) and positively associated with positive experiences ( β = 0.268, p < 0.001); the negative association between hindrance stressors and creative self-efficacy was significant ( β = −0.107, p = 0.043). Mediation analysis indicated that creative self-efficacy played a significant mediating role only in the path involving challenge stressors (indirect effect = 0.023, 95% CI [0.007, 0.044]) and was not significant in the path involving hindrance stressors; positive experiences significantly served as a mediator in the relationships between both challenge stressors (indirect effect = 0.042, 95% CI [0.020, 0.068]) and hindrance stressors (indirect effect = 0.019, 95% CI [0.003, 0.039]) on AI dependence. The chain mediation effects did not reach significance in either path. Conclusion The study found asymmetry in the dual pathways by which Challenge and Hindrance stressors relate to AI dependence. These findings extend the I-PACE model to the issue of AI dependence in arts education and provide empirical evidence and intervention insights for targeted prevention of problematic AI use.

item.title: Exploring antecedents and consequences of value co-creation of women entrepreneurs: a conceptual framework and research agenda
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
This study examines the antecedents and outcomes of value co-creation among women entrepreneurs, emphasizing the importance of addressing the unique challenges they encounter in entrepreneurial activities. While prior studies have investigated women's entrepreneurial motivations and barriers, the concept of value co-creation in this context remains insufficiently explored, thereby limiting theoretical development in the field. This conceptual paper develops a model derived from an extensive, critical, and multidisciplinary literature review. The review synthesizes insights from entrepreneurship, management, and network theory to explain how individual dynamic capabilities, opportunity recognition, entrepreneurial orientation, and entrepreneurial networks collectively foster value co-creation among women entrepreneurs. The study identifies four key antecedents of value co-creation: individual dynamic capabilities, opportunity recognition, entrepreneurial orientation, and entrepreneurial networks. It also proposes that value co-creation positively influences business performance. The study introduces an integrative conceptual framework and formulates five testable hypotheses to guide future empirical research. The paper provides theoretical and practical insights for policymakers and entrepreneurship support organizations to enhance women's entrepreneurial success through value co-creation strategies.

item.title: AI vs. human authorship in paintings: Differential impacts on consumers' perceived value
item.description:
Computers in Human Behavior Reports
The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) art generators has introduced algorithmically created paintings into mainstream consumer markets, yet consumers consistently assign lower value to AI-generated works than to human-created equivalents. This paper proposes perceived creative authenticity---consumers' subjective perception that an artwork reflects a genuine creative process characterized by human-centered values of originality, craftsmanship, and uniqueness---as a theoretically distinct mechanism explaining this value differential. Conceptually differentiated from perceived creativity, which concerns the novelty of the artistic output, perceived creative authenticity addresses the genuineness of the creator-work relationship. Drawing on authenticity theory and Psychological Ownership Theory, we develop a moderated mediation framework hypothesizing that (H1) human authorship elicits higher perceived value than AI authorship, (H2) perceived creative authenticity mediates this effect, while the indirect effects through perceived creativity, perceived effort, and anthropocentric creativity beliefs are not significant, establishing perceived creative authenticity as the primary explanatory mechanism within the tested model, and (H3) non-fungible token (NFT) authentication attenuates the mediated pathway by providing verifiable creative provenance. Across five studies, results support this framework: Study 1 conceptually replicates the human-AI value gap among Chinese consumers; Studies 2a—2c demonstrate the mediating role of perceived creative authenticity: Study 2a establishes the basic mediation pathway; Study 2b shows through parallel mediation that perceived creative authenticity uniquely mediates the effect while perceived creativity, perceived effort, and anthropocentric creativity beliefs do not exhibit significant indirect effects; and Study 2c provides causal evidence through a moderation-of-process design; and Study 3 shows that NFT authentication narrows the authenticity gap between human and AI art. These findings advance the literature on human-computer interaction by identifying process-based authenticity judgments as a key psychological mechanism shaping consumer responses to algorithmic creative products, with implications for artists and platforms navigating digital art markets.

item.title: Prolonged participation AI-based mindfulness school programme in primary education: Implications for AI practices, schools and developers
item.description:
Learning and Instruction
Background Research on Artificial Intelligence (AI) -supported mindfulness programs in primary education remains limited, particularly in rural contexts where implementation conditions differ from urban settings. Aim This study examines the effects of an AI-supported mindfulness intervention on rural primary school students' behavioral and socio-emotional outcomes, and on teachers' self-regulation and creativity, measured at pretest (T1), posttest (T2), and follow-up (T3). Method The study used a quasi-experimental design with a control group across selected classrooms in four rural schools. The sample comprised an intervention group ( N = 91) and a control group ( N = 54), with 16 teachers participating in the intervention group. The intervention ran for ten weekly sessions across the fall and spring semesters. AI tools (ChatGPT and Gemini) supported teacher candidates in lesson planning and in the inquiry phase that followed each mindfulness practice. Implementation fidelity, assessed through mentor cross-rating, was 88.6% ( SD = 9.7), with Cohen's κ = .86 in a sub-sample. Results Split-plot ANOVAs showed significant Time × Group interactions favouring the intervention group on life skills (LSAS, η 2 p = .242), behavioural difficulties (SDQ total, η 2 p = .378), and teacher-student relationship quality (STRS total, η 2 p = .025). In the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ), all five subscales were significant. The Closeness subscale drove the STRS effect; Conflict did not change. Nested analyses confirmed consistent effects across grade levels. Teachers showed gains on all nine TSRS subscales, and on the Social Value subscale of the TCS. Conclusion The intervention was associated with improvements in students' life skills, behavioral functioning, and teacher-student closeness, as well as gains in teachers' self-regulation. The findings inform AI-supported mindfulness practice in rural primary education.

item.title: More than we can make: generative AI, artistic forms, and artistic becoming
item.description:
AI & Society
Abstract Debates surrounding generative AI and creativity have largely focused on artifacts: who or what produced a given image or text, whether machine outputs qualify as art, and how authorship and value should be understood. Drawing on aesthetics, craft theory, anthropology, human–computer interaction, hybrid craft, digital fabrication, and rematerialization, this article argues that art has historically involved two intertwined dimensions. Artistic forms stabilize and transmit meaning through artifacts, whereas artistic becoming refers to the developmental and transformative processes through which new possibilities of perception, interpretation, and experience emerge, in makers, in recipients, and in cultures. The article’s central claim is a decoupling thesis: for most of history these dimensions were contingently coupled, since producing sophisticated forms required the maker’s becoming, and generative AI loosens this coupling by enabling such forms to emerge without the specific developmental pathways that traditionally conditioned them. Rather than signaling the disappearance of creativity, the decoupling relocates to new sites and makes visible dimensions of artistic practice that the demands of production long obscured. The article situates generative AI within a longer history of hybridization and distributed creativity, develops the decoupling thesis across these three levels, and defends a normative orientation: under conditions of symbolic abundance, the creative practices most worth pursuing are those that route generative fluency back into embodied, situated experience.

item.title: Generative AI in creative education: baseline-linked evidence on learning processes, artistic performance, and authorship
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly shaping creative learning in higher education art courses, yet its educational value remains contested when creative support, output generation, authorship, and skill development become intertwined. This study investigates AI-supported creative learning in an undergraduate art course. Methods: The study used linked data from 133 students, including prior course performance, final creative-performance assessment, and post-project questionnaire responses. AI use was operationalized through two dimensions: assistive use for ideation, refinement, process management, and technique learning, and content-generative use involving AI contributions to creative output. The analysis combined baseline-adjusted outcome models, performance-change models, propensity-score adjustment, AI-use intensity comparisons, and robustness checks across alternative AI-use definitions. Results: The findings show a clear process-outcome decoupling pattern. AI use was associated with stronger perceived support and skill transfer, while final artistic performance and baseline-to-final performance change showed no corresponding improvement. Content-generative AI use was associated with lower evaluated authorship, suggesting that AI-shaped artifacts may reduce the visibility of students' creative decision-making in final outcomes. Discussion: The study contributes a differentiated account of AI in creative education and argues that responsible AI integration should focus on how students use, document, justify, and reflect on AI within the creative process.

item.title: Generative AI ‐Supported Creative Writing Among Primary School Students: A Study of Creative Writing Performance, Writing Self‐Efficacy, and Flow State
item.description:
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning
ABSTRACT Background The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into creative writing is a growing trend. However, few studies have examined primary school students' interactions with GenAI alongside their writing experiences and resulting writing products. Objectives This study compared creative writing performance, writing self‐efficacy, and flow state across GenAI‐supported, peer‐collaborative and individual writing conditions. It also descriptively examined patterns of student–AI interaction during the writing activity. Methods An experiment involved 78 primary school students in China assigned to three conditions: GenAI‐supported writing ( n = 20), peer collaboration ( n = 38; 19 pairs), and individual writing ( n = 20). Results and Conclusions Students in the GenAI‐supported writing group obtained higher creative writing performance scores than those in the peer‐collaborative and individual writing groups. Interaction analysis showed that students mainly used GenAI to generate and elaborate ideas. Among episodes with observable uptake, adapted or selective incorporation was more common than direct incorporation, and no complete GenAI response was reproduced verbatim. In addition, students in the GenAI‐supported writing group also reported higher writing self‐efficacy than those in the individual writing group, although the difference from the peer‐collaborative writing group was not significant. However, they reported the lowest flow state. Writing self‐efficacy was positively associated with creative writing performance, whereas no significant association between flow state and creative writing performance was observed in this sample. These findings suggest that GenAI may serve as a resource for developing ideas in primary school creative writing.

item.title: Generative artificial intelligence in jazz improvisation: an Actor-Network Theory perspective
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) plays an increasingly significant role in the artistic creation process. In the domain of highly interactive human-machine composition, GAI is no longer a passive tool but exhibits a certain degree of agency. Based on Actor-Network Theory (ANT), a social science theoretical framework proposed by French sociologist Bruno Latour and other scholars, GAI can be viewed as a non-human subject endowed with the status of an actor. In jazz improvisation, a representative creative activity, the agency of GAI is manifested in the generation of its specific musical works, presenting a contrast to human creation. Furthermore, this process reveals the leading and constraining factors in the actions of GAI, as well as the potential pathways and mutual interactions of its future co-creative development with humans.

item.title: How do we measure creativity? A systematic review and taxonomy of evaluative methods in human-AI co-creativity
item.description:
Human-Computer Interaction
As artificial intelligence (AI) rapidly integrates as a cognitive partner in day-to-day creative tasks, to truly understand the value and effects of this integration, it is critical to know how co-creativity is defined, measured, and understood. Without a coherent understanding of the evaluative practices in the field, it is challenging for researchers to determine which metrics are appropriate, for practitioners to adopt effective evaluative methods, and for the field to build cumulative knowledge. To address this pressing need, we conduct a systematic review of Human-AI (HAI) co-creativity measurement metrics and evaluative methods. Through a critical analysis of how creativity is conceptualized and measured, we synthesize existing evaluation practices into a taxonomy for interpreting HAI co-creativity research. This taxonomy provides a multidimensional framework for interpreting how creativity is operationalized across the literature. By mapping these measurement patterns and gaps, this study ultimately offers researchers and practitioners a deeper understanding of how creativity can be meaningfully assessed in Human-AI co-creative tasks and provides a starting point for the development of more rigorous and context-sensitive measurement strategies for HAI co-creativity and cognitive support.

item.title: Prospective predictors of generative AI initiation, engagement, and problematic use among Japanese adults: a two-wave study
item.description:
Computers in Human Behavior Reports
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) adoption is rising rapidly, but how its determinants extend beyond first-level access into within-user engagement and problematic use remains poorly understood, and almost all existing evidence is cross-sectional. Using two consecutive waves of the Japan COVID-19 and Society Internet Survey (2024 baseline; 2025 follow-up), we examined 49 baseline characteristics — organized with Resources and Appropriation Theory (RAT) as a taxonomy of personal, positional, and resource-based factors of (a) generative AI initiation during 2025 among 9,411 baseline never-users and, among 2,490 new-onset users, (b) use intensity, three purpose composites (productivity/creative, daily-life/information, social/emotional), and (c) problematic AI use measured with the 11-item Problematic ChatGPT Use Scale. All predictors were measured at the baseline wave. Twenty directional expectations were separated from exploratory screening; 17 were supported. Three findings stand out. First, the correlates of adoption and within-user engagement only partially overlapped across all three RAT domains, with several factors — age, graduate education, employment role, and device type — differentiating not only whether people adopted but also what they used AI for. Second, daily-life/information use was largely undifferentiated by age, education, income, employment role, or device type, suggesting an egalitarian leading-edge use case alongside more stratified productivity, social/emotional, and problematic-use domains. Third, problematic AI use was distinct from heavy use on two complementary criteria — measurement-level non-identity and a divergent predictor profile — with predictor profiles diverging across male, agreeableness, and heavy PC/tablet use. Equity-oriented governance of generative AI should monitor not only access and intensity but also the qualitative engagement profile of use.

item.title: Generative AI in K-12 creative writing instruction: A systematic review and narrative synthesis
item.description:
Acta Psychologica
Generative AI is rapidly entering writing instruction in public education; however, a systematic, quality-appraised synthesis of its effects on K-12 students' creative writing is lacking. This review synthesises and critically appraises the empirical evidence, using a scaffolding-versus-substitution framework to distinguish AI-assisted performance from the development of students' own writing. We searched seven databases without language restrictions for 2020-2026, following PRISMA 2020. Risk of bias and methodological quality were assessed with ROBINS-I, RoB 2 and CASP, the certainty of evidence with GRADE and GRADE-CERQual, and findings were synthesised without meta-analysis (SWiM), stratified by design. Seventeen studies met the criteria (total N = 736). All six comparisons of AI-supported with non-AI instruction favoured AI on text quality or creativity, but in every study the scored texts were produced with AI access or under unreported conditions; no study assessed AI-free or delayed writing performance. Effects on writing-related affect were mixed, and no intervention reported a planned withdrawal of AI support. Observational process data indicated that students used AI input to develop their ideas when they retained control, but that AI could also steer the narrative or supply text adopted with little reworking. No study was at low risk of bias, and the certainty of evidence was very low for all quantitative outcomes. The evidence therefore describes what students produce with AI rather than what they learn to do without it; studies with AI-free post-tests, delayed transfer measures and planned fading of support are needed. The protocol was pre-registered (PROSPERO: CRD420261303257).
